deep.reconstruction:
The page has two unrelated blocks: spherical trigonometry and rotations in the left column and at the bottom, and binary quadratic forms in the middle. The polyhedron counting on the previous page is not continued.

A. LEFT COLUMN / BOTTOM: rotations given by Euler angles.

Notation. The symbol p^q r is best read as the rotation R_z(p) R_x(q) R_z(r), i.e. Euler angles in z-x-z order. Juxtaposition (written '+') means composition.

Last line. Riemann writes p^q r = (p+pi)^(-q)(r+pi). This is the standard two-to-one ambiguity of Euler angles. It holds because R_z(pi) R_x(-q) R_z(pi) = R_x(q).

Triangle closure. The lines read 'pi-A ^b pi-C ^a pi-B ^c a' and 'pi-A ^b pi-C = -c_(B-pi) -a'. They express a 'turtle walk' around a spherical triangle with sides a, b, c and angles A, B, C:
- R_z(c) R_x(pi-A) R_z(b) R_x(pi-C) R_z(a) R_x(pi-B) = 1;
- equivalently R_x(pi-A) R_z(b) R_x(pi-C) = R_z(-c) R_x(B-pi) R_z(-a), with orientation conventions assumed.
This is the classical link between products of rotations and spherical triangles.

Problem: when do two Euler rotations commute? Riemann asks when (p,q,r)(p1,q1,r1) = (p1,q1,r1)(p,q,r).
- The product reduces to the middle factor R_x(q) R_z(r+p1) R_x(q1), which closes a spherical triangle.
- Set q = pi-A, q1 = pi-C, and r+p1 = r1+p = b.
- The two orders give mirror-image triangles. Commutation then needs p-p1 = r-r1 (equivalently p-r = p1-r1) to equal the difference of the two outer sides.
- That difference is fixed by Napier's analogy: tan((p-p1)/2)/tan(b/2) = sin((q-q1)/2)/sin((q+q1)/2). Here sin((q+q1)/2) = sin((A+C)/2).
- The second condition is sin((r+p)/2)/tan(q/2) = sin((r1+p1)/2)/tan(q1/2).
- The composite is p2^(q2) r2 with q2 = B-pi, p2 = p-c, r2 = r-c.
- The partly legible side bookkeeping is p1-p = r1-r = a-c, p+r = a+b+c, p1+r1 = a+b-c, p2+r2 = -a+b-c.

Meaning of the two invariants (my modern explanation). The unit quaternion of R_z(p)R_x(q)R_z(r) is:
(cos(q/2)cos((p+r)/2), sin(q/2)cos((p-r)/2), sin(q/2)sin((p-r)/2), cos(q/2)sin((p+r)/2)).
So the rotation axis has azimuth n/2, where n = p-r. Its latitude s satisfies tan s = sin((p+r)/2)/tan(q/2). Riemann sets for all three rotations:
- sin((p+r)/2)/tan(q/2) = sin((p1+r1)/2)/tan(q1/2) = sin((p2+r2)/2)/tan(q2/2) = tan s;
- p-r = p1-r1 = p2-r2 = n.
This is exactly the statement that the three rotations are coaxial.

Half rotation angles. Riemann introduces alpha, gamma, beta, the half rotation angles of the three rotations:
- cos(alpha) = cos(q/2)cos((p+r)/2), which is the quaternion scalar part;
- sin(alpha) = sin(q/2)/cos(s);
- cot(alpha) = sin(s) cot((p+r)/2), where the transcription has 'sin q';
- and the same for gamma with (p1,q1,r1) and beta with (p2,q2,r2).
He concludes cot(beta) = -cot(alpha+gamma), sin(beta) = sin(alpha+gamma) and cos(beta) = -cos(alpha+gamma). So beta = pi - (alpha+gamma): coaxial rotations compose by adding angles, up to his sign conventions for the third rotation.

Bottom block. Cases I and II give sign variants of the commutation conditions:
- Case I: r+p1 = r1+p = pi-B, p-p1 = r-r1 = C-A.
- Case II: r+p1 = -r1-p = pi-B, p1-p = A+C, r1-r = -A-C.
- Further lines include p = -r and pi-B = A+C.
The line -r1^(-q1)(-p1) is the inverse of p1^(q1) r1. Case II probably handles the degenerate solution of half-turns about perpendicular axes, in which pi-B = A+C appears.

B. MIDDLE: representations by an indefinite binary quadratic form.

Setting. Take the form f = a x^2 + 2b xy + c y^2 in Gauss's notation, with D = b^2 - ac > 0. Let (t,u) satisfy t^2 - D u^2 = omega^2, where omega is the divisor of the form. Gauss's automorphs carry a representation (alpha, gamma) of m = f(alpha,gamma) to:
- x' = ((t - b u) alpha - c u gamma)/omega;
- y' = (a u alpha + (t + b u) gamma)/omega.
The struck-out lines 'x = alpha(t+b..) + gamma(cu)' are a first attempt at this.

Power-of-unit parametrisation. Riemann writes t_n = omega(w+v)/2 and u_n sqrt(D) = omega(w-v)/2. Hence:
- w = (t_n + u_n sqrt D)/omega and v = (t_n - u_n sqrt D)/omega;
- w v = 1, so w = epsilon^n for a unit epsilon.
Substituting gives
- x_n = [w(alpha sqrt D - alpha b - gamma c) + v(alpha sqrt D + alpha b + gamma c)]/(2 sqrt D);
- y_n = [w(gamma sqrt D + alpha a + gamma b) + v(gamma sqrt D - alpha a - gamma b)]/(2 sqrt D).
This is the closed, Binet-type form of the whole orbit of representations.

Eliminating v. He forms (alpha sqrt D + alpha b + gamma c) y_n + (alpha a + gamma b - gamma sqrt D) x_n. The v-terms cancel identically. The w-coefficient reduces to w(alpha^2 a + 2 alpha gamma b + gamma^2 c) = w m. That line is crossed out but correct; Riemann's bracketed intermediate expansion is messy.

Linear factors. He factors m = (1/a)(alpha a + gamma b - gamma sqrt D)(alpha a + gamma b + gamma sqrt D), using D = b^2 - ac. He then writes a second factorisation over c.

Final identity. a x_n + y_n(sqrt D + b) = (1/omega)(alpha a + gamma(sqrt D + b))(t_n + u_n sqrt D). That is, the quadratic-irrational element attached to the representation is multiplied by the unit (t + u sqrt D)/omega. This is the standard ideal-theoretic or Dirichlet view of the automorph action.

C. Sketches. There is a rhombus-like quadrilateral labelled with p, q, r and angles, and a triangle A, B, C. These illustrate the composition/triangle bookkeeping. A larger quadrilateral with numbered vertices and diagonals is unrelated.
errors: The line transcribed 'cot alpha = sin q cot((p+r)/2)' (and its analogues) is wrong as transcribed. The correct identity, consistent with Riemann's other lines, is cot(alpha) = sin(s) cot((p+r)/2): from sin(alpha) = sin(q/2)/cos(s) and cos(alpha) = cos(q/2)cos((p+r)/2) one gets exactly sin(s)cot((p+r)/2). Most likely 'q' is a misreading of 's'.

The second factorisation 'w (1/c)(gamma c + alpha b + alpha sqrt D)(alpha a + gamma b - gamma sqrt D)' is not equal to w m as transcribed: the product contains sqrt(D) terms. The correct form is (1/c)(gamma c + alpha(b + sqrt D))(gamma c + alpha(b - sqrt D)). This is either a slip or a misreading of the second factor.

Riemann's bracketed intermediate expansion ('alpha gamma (sqrt D - b)^2 - alpha gamma a c + ...') is garbled or incomplete. The struck-out result w(alpha^2 a + gamma^2 c + 2 alpha gamma b) is nevertheless correct.
In the top formula the denominator must be tan((r+p1)/2) = tan(b/2) for Napier's analogy. If it really read tan((r-r1)/2), the ratio would be trivially 1 given p-p1 = r-r1.

The signs for the third rotation (q2 = B-pi, -sin(beta) = ..., cos(beta) = -cos(alpha+gamma)) encode the composite only up to the quaternion sign and orientation conventions. The relation beta = pi - (alpha+gamma) means 2 beta = -2(alpha+gamma) mod 2 pi, which is consistent but not self-evidently the product rather than its inverse.

The side bookkeeping 'p+r = a+b+c, p1+r1 = a+b-c' is not fully consistent with the tan s equalities under the usual half-perimeter formulas. Either the reading or the assignment of sides is uncertain; it may be a slip.

results.what: Two-to-one ambiguity of z-x-z Euler angles: (p,q,r) and (p+pi,-q,r+pi) give the same rotation
Product of three rotations around a spherical triangle; R_x(pi-A)R_z(b)R_x(pi-C) = R_z(-c)R_x(B-pi)R_z(-a)
results.modern_name: Composition of rotations via spherical triangles (Rodrigues/Hamilton construction)

results.what: Commutation conditions for two Euler-angle rotations, derived with Napier's analogy
results.modern_name: Commuting rotations are coaxial; Napier's analogies
results.usually_credited_to: Napier (1614) for the analogies; commutation criterion classical (Rodrigues 1840)

results.what: Rotation axis of R_z(p)R_x(q)R_z(r) has azimuth (p-r)/2 and latitude s with tan s = sin((p+r)/2)/tan(q/2); half-angle alpha with cos(alpha) = cos(q/2)cos((p+r)/2); coaxial rotations add angles
All representations of m by an indefinite form (a,b,c) from one solution via automorphs, x_n, y_n written as w-, v-linear combinations (w = epsilon^n, v = epsilon^-n)
results.modern_name: Automorphs of binary quadratic forms / Pell equation orbit of representations

results.what: a x_n + (b + sqrt D) y_n = (1/omega)(alpha a + gamma(b + sqrt D))(t_n + u_n sqrt D)
results.modern_name: Action of the unit group on the module element a x + (b + sqrt D) y; ideal-form correspondence

deep.surprise_reason: Both blocks are textbook material by the 1850s. Euler-angle composition and commutation via spherical triangles goes back to Euler and Rodrigues, with Napier's analogies. The automorph and Pell orbit of representations follows Gauss and Dirichlet. The quaternion-like axis/half-angle formulas are a neat private derivation, but they are not new relative to Rodrigues (1840).

transcription_corrections: Line 'cot alpha = sin q cot((p+r)/2)' and its analogues: the factor is almost certainly 'sin s' (s defined by tan s = sin((p+r)/2)/tan(q/2)), not 'sin q'.
Top formula denominator: likely 'tg 1/2 (r+p_1)' (= tan(b/2), as Napier's analogy requires), not 'tg 1/2 (r-r_1)'.
'= \mathfrak{b}' after the struck line is presumably '= m' (the represented number f(alpha,gamma)) or a similar symbol; mathematically it must equal w*f(alpha,gamma).
'r_1+p_1 = pi_1' is unclear; it may be another side relation such as r_1+p_1 = b-type bookkeeping.
Second factorisation: the second factor should probably read (gamma c + alpha b - alpha sqrt D) rather than (alpha a + gamma b - gamma sqrt D).
